hero.label: Founder & former CEO, LessonWise (now Alucea)
hero.headline: I spent seven years building a subscription AI tutoring platform from the ground up.
hero.intro: I came up with LessonWise, founded it and took it through three pivots to BrightPath: a tutoring service where AI analyses every lesson and a person signs it off. BrightPath is live today and still serves families. This site shows who I am, how I work and what I learned on the way.

journey.heading: Engineer, teacher, founder.
journey.intro: I trained as a mechanical engineer, taught maths for more than a decade, and spent seven years taking a company through every stage: the idea, the launch, three pivots, fundraising, growth and handover.

items.title: Mechanical engineer at Herrenknecht
items.text: Trained as a mechanical engineer, then designed drilling systems and machine elements at Herrenknecht, delivering client projects to specification, all in German.

items.title: A second degree, in music
items.text: Moved to London to study music, something I had always wanted to do. Alongside it I began tutoring maths: nearly 5,000 hours of one-to-one teaching since.

items.title: LessonWise: a platform for tutors to teach groups online
items.text: Wrote a 200-page product requirements document covering every user journey and feature, ran a tender, and led an offshore team to launch. The platform had a classroom built for large groups; payments tied to each lesson taking place, with tutors paid within 72 hours; messaging that let students find each other and form groups for courses; homework and assessment tools; and a profile page where tutors could promote themselves and launch their own courses. About 200 tutors joined within months, from several countries, so I worked with our payment provider and developers to get tutor payouts working country by country.

items.title: Tutors did not want to build their own audience
items.text: So we found the students for them. Free masterclasses fed paid courses, and more than 4,000 students joined within four months. That traction brought in our first significant investment, initially as shareholder loans.

items.title: One-to-one first
items.text: Narrowed the offer to one-to-one tuition to build a base of families who trusted us before going wider. In parallel I applied for an Innovate UK Smart grant, and ran free maths masterclasses through community organisations.

items.title: Back to a team of one, then up again
items.text: Ran the company alone for months: teaching, selling, keeping investors and stakeholders informed, and directing marketing freelancers. Found an acquisition channel that worked and hired a sales team. The following year was our peak growth.

items.title: BrightPath: managed tutoring with AI in every lesson
items.text: Short-term exam customers did not stay. I redesigned the business around families who wanted their child's learning managed, on subscription, with evidence of progress every month. I also set up an offshore support team to give families faster answers.

items.title: BrightPath live with paying families
items.text: BrightPath was live with paying families, and I moved our tutors onto it myself, inviting each one to an onboarding session. A multinational company signed a 12-month staff training plan with us. In September 2026 I handed the company to a new leadership team. It continues today as Alucea.

work.heading: Five problems, and how I solved them.
work.intro: Each one covers the problem, the decisions I made and what happened. Full specifications are available on request.

breadth.heading: A founder does every job at least once.

items.title: Product
items.text: Wrote the full set of product requirements, with user stories, acceptance criteria and data rules, and ran daily product reviews of the build against them.

items.title: AI and automation
items.text: Human-in-the-loop design, retrieval-grounded chat and evaluation targets on Google Gemini models.

items.title: Technical delivery
items.text: Managed engineering vendors across the UK, India and the Philippines, and commissioned a code audit of four codebases.

items.title: Fundraising and investors
items.text: Raised £1.6 million in equity and debt, reported to investors every month and built the 2026–2030 business plan.

items.title: Team
items.text: Hired and led a peak team of 18 across three countries, in sales, marketing, support and engineering, including an offshore support team. Second-round candidates did a written work sample.

items.title: Finance and operations
items.text: Ran bookkeeping, financial reporting and grant applications, and two R&D tax credit claims documenting the platform's technical work.

items.title: Safeguarding and data
items.text: Built the safeguarding framework and the access and GDPR rules for children's data, including identity and right-to-work checks for tutors.

items.title: Partnerships
items.text: Delivered free group tutoring to disadvantaged pupils in Ireland with the charity Teach One, Save One, on our platform at no cost, and set up a simple way for it to sell its lesson recordings.

items.title: Grants and public funding
items.text: Applied twice for an Innovate UK Smart grant, narrowly missing the second time, and prepared two R&D tax credit claims.

items.title: Marketing and growth
items.text: Tested campaigns before scaling them, tracked each one back to the leads it brought in, had tutors record worked exam answers on our whiteboard for social media, offered a free 68-question GCSE diagnostic test with personal feedback, and ran free community masterclasses that brought in families.

items.title: B2B and charity sales
items.text: Bid for a national charity's tutoring tender, and won a 12-month staff training plan with a multinational company, and designed an English course with medical vocabulary for an employer's overseas staff.

lessons.heading: Six things I would tell my 2019 self.

items.title: Ship the simple version first.
items.text: Our first platform had too many features, and many were never needed. I would go to market sooner with less, and let customers tell me what to add.

items.title: Hire slowly, and never out of pressure.
items.text: We grew the team too fast, too early, and under stress I hired reactively. Now I hire for a need I can already see, not one I hope for.

items.title: Only accept accountability that comes with authority.
items.text: For too long I answered for outcomes I did not have the power to change. I now check that the two match before I say yes, and I put the right protections in place on day one.

items.title: Say the hard thing early.
items.text: There were times I stayed quiet when I should have pushed back. A problem raised early is small. Raised late, it is expensive.

items.title: Write everything down.
items.text: Keep a record of decisions every week and every month. It keeps you honest, and it is the first thing you reach for when things get hard.

items.title: No company is worth your health.
items.text: Years without a real break left me tired, reactive and a worse leader. I now treat rest, and knowing when to change course, as part of the job.

how.heading: How I work.
how.intro: Measured across six years of my own sent email, and shown in what I did with it.

stats.label: of replies sent within an hour

items.title: When a customer is hurt, I act that evening.
items.text: A browser update once broke the audio in our classroom mid-lesson. I escalated within minutes, refunded the families and paid the tutor myself, then moved a full upgrade into the Christmas break, when lessons were quiet.

items.title: I test it myself.
items.text: I tested the new whiteboard for an hour on the day of the demo, sent notes with a screen recording, and set the release date by when tutors needed training. When some payments did not unlock a student's enrolment, I had the whole team test the Google Pay checkout on desktop and mobile within four days, with screen recordings.

items.title: I write the first draft myself.
items.text: For an Innovate UK grant, I wrote the technical answers over a weekend, before the grant writer was back from holiday.

items.title: I treat a no as data.
items.text: Innovate UK turned us down. I asked straight away to go through the assessors' feedback, found the gap and resubmitted. We missed again, by a small margin. When Google for Startups first declined our cloud credits application, I sent their team the evidence they needed and asked them to reconsider. A week later we were accepted, with $25,000 of credits.

items.title: I test before I spend.
items.text: Before scaling our marketing, I ran a test across eight courses to find what worked, and kept to one subject area.

items.title: I scope from the customer's real numbers.
items.text: Before pricing a tender for a national education charity, I asked for their peak number of live sessions and users, so the quote matched how they actually taught.

items.title: I look for the deal both sides can say yes to.
items.text: I swapped a supplier's two-month deposit for an earlier payment date, and offered a client the option to fund development and get it back as platform credit.

items.title: I sell, and I say no when it is right.
items.text: Free community masterclasses brought in families. One enquiry became a matched trial lesson within the hour. When a family needed face-to-face lessons we could not offer, I pointed them to a local tutor.

items.title: I onboard people myself.
items.text: From a tutor's first call to a trial lesson with a student took three days, with their criminal record certificate checked the next morning.

items.title: When a client is unhappy, I change course that week.
items.text: A company felt its group English course was not meeting each learner's needs. I wrote up what they told me, moved them to one-to-one lessons the following week, and matched them with a tutor focused on conversation. They carried on with us.
